cim: Back-to-back cyber incidents at US financial investigators and spy agencies follow a string of federal hacks and outages
cim_eredeti: Back-to-back cyber incidents at US financial investigators and spy agencies follow a string of federal hacks and outages
szoveg_eredeti:
The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) took systems offline as a precaution after unauthorized access. Hours earlier, reports emerged of a separate breach at the CIA and other US intelligence agencies that may have involved an AI tool.

FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident. The Verge reported that the agency announced on Tuesday that a limited portion of its systems had been accessed without authorization.

While FinCEN didn't disclose the scope or cause of the incident, it took some systems offline as a precaution. FinCEN's mission is to protect the financial system from illegal activity such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It also manages financial transaction data for law enforcement and collects suspicious activity reports from banks under the Bank Secrecy Act.

Banks can still file suspicious activity reports online, FinCEN says, though some services may face delays. Its telephone hotline for financial institutions isn't affected, the agency says.

The New York Times reported a breach at several US intelligence agencies just hours before FinCEN's announcement, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. According to the Times, the intrusion hit the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

The report said intruders broke into an analysis system for open-source intelligence that searches publicly available, unclassified information to produce intelligence. That includes commercially available datasets, social media content, satellite imagery, and other online material, according to the report. Even though much of this data is freely available or sold by data brokers, it can be revealing when combined, the Times noted.

It's still not clear what specific data was accessed or taken. Classified information wasn't at risk, sources told the Times. One person familiar with the matter said the issue has since been resolved, and an ODNI representative said critical capabilities weren't affected.

Multiple sources told the New York Times that investigators suspect the attackers behind the intelligence breach used Artex, an AI hacking tool. A Chinese engineer released the tool in July to help organizations defend against cyberattacks. US officials and security experts say attackers have since repurposed it for offensive use.

Cybersecurity researchers have linked Artex to dozens of attacks on companies worldwide since its release, including in Japan and South Korea. Investigators haven't yet determined who was behind the US intelligence breach. Early indicators, including the use of Artex, point to possible Chinese involvement, according to two people familiar with the matter. Western officials have accused Chinese intelligence services and a network of contractors of cyberattacks on US agencies and companies for years, allegations Beijing routinely denies.

These reports come during a stretch of frequent technical outages and security incidents across federal agencies. Attacks aren't always the cause, and in some cases, fear of an attack triggered the disruptions. US officials told the New York Times that AI had uncovered software flaws that needed to be patched quickly. A few of those efforts produced errors.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) reported a security incident just last week and took several internal applications offline, Nextgov said. President Donald Trump confirmed a hack of the FBI's National Crime Information Center on Saturday during a phone interview with Fox News. CNN had earlier reported the breach of the nationwide database, which law enforcement agencies use to share information on suspects. The FBI is investigating.

Other disruptions, which officials and companies say weren't caused by cyberattacks, have added to public concern. Those include a multi-day outage of the NSA's internal classified network last week and a nationwide ground stop this month that officials blamed on router maintenance issues.

Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence who Trump recently tapped as acting cyber director, tried to reassure the public on several US news shows on Sunday. Speaking on ABC's "This Week," Clayton said cyber espionage and security incidents have long been part of American business and daily life.
